title: Deacons and the Seven
lead: The Greek diakonos means "servant" or "agent." In the New Testament letters it names a recognized helper in the local church, alongside the overseers (Philippians 1:1; 1 Timothy 3:8–13). Christian tradition traces the office to the Seven chosen in Acts 6, though Acts never calls them deacons, and the churches still differ on what a deacon is.

sections.b: The diakon- word family covers service at tables, care for the needy and service of the word (Acts 6:1–4; Luke 22:26–27). Jesus calls himself one who serves (Luke 22:27). Paul calls himself and his coworkers diakonoi of the new covenant (2 Corinthians 3:6), greets the overseers and deacons at Philippi (Philippians 1:1), and commends Phoebe, "deacon" (or "servant") of the church at Cenchreae (Romans 16:1). The Pastoral Letters list the qualities required of deacons, and of "women" who may be deacons or deacons' wives (1 Timothy 3:8–13). John Collins and others have argued that the word stresses being an authorized agent, not only humble service.
sections.refs: Luke 22:26–27; Acts 6:1–6; Romans 16:1; 2 Corinthians 3:6; Philippians 1:1; 1 Timothy 3:8–13

sections.b: By the end of the first century, 1 Clement speaks of bishops and deacons appointed by the apostles (1 Clement 42), and Ignatius of Antioch, about AD 110, names three ranks: bishop, presbyters and deacons. Irenaeus calls Stephen "the first deacon." Deacons served the bishop, cared for the poor, read the Gospel and assisted at the Eucharist. Women deacons are attested in the Eastern churches for several centuries.
